column2: How do I animate a presentation (transitions, builds, magic move)?
column3: In the presentation, “✨ Animate” tab on the right. The transition plays when arriving on the slide: fade, dissolve, fade through black, push, slide, reveal, wipe, zoom, swap, flip, cube, or “magic move”: duplicate the slide (⧉), move, enlarge or rotate the objects on the copy, and they glide from one place to the other during playback (objects with the same name work too). Choose an object then “＋ Build in” or “＋ Build out”: appear, fade, arrive from one side, grow, bounce, drop, wipe, blur, swirl, typewriter for a text; each animation starts on click, with the previous one or after it, with its duration and its delay; “Animation order” arranges them (↑ ↓) and “▶ Preview” shows them.

column2: How do I present with my notes, the next slide and a timer?
column3: In the presentation: “▶ Play” (from the beginning, or “⏵ From here”) goes full screen; → space or click: next, ←: previous, a number then Enter: go to that slide, B: black screen, W: white screen, L: laser pointer, Esc: quit. “🎤 Presenter” (or P during playback) opens a second window to put on your screen: the current slide, the next one (or the remaining animations), your notes (A− A+), the timer and the time. Notes are written under the slide (📝 Notes) or in the Slide tab. A slide can also move on to the next by itself, and the presentation can loop (kiosk, exhibition).

column2: How do I import a PowerPoint, a LibreOffice file, Keynote or a PDF?
column3: Lists → Editing tools → “🎞️ Presentation and slideshow” → “⤒ Import a presentation”, or “⤒ Import” in an open presentation (added after the slide shown, or in its place). PowerPoint (.pptx) and OpenDocument / LibreOffice Impress (.odp): each slide with its texts in place (sizes, bold, colours, lists), its images (stored in Media), its shapes, its tables, its charts, its notes and its transitions. Keynote (.key) has a closed format: in Keynote, File → Export to → PowerPoint, then import the .pptx. A PDF gives its images (scans, photos), one per slide: its text cannot be read here. Also: photos (one slide per photo), a text or Markdown (“# Title” starts a slide, “-” makes a bullet, “---” separates, “Notes:” the notes) and the .json file of a presentation from the app.

column2: How do I export a presentation as PDF, images or video?
column3: In the presentation, “⤓ Export”: PDF or printing (one slide per page, or with the speaker notes under each slide; in the print window, choose “Save as PDF”), the slide shown as PNG, all the slides as PNG (a .zip file), a WebM video (each slide for its duration, with the music; to keep in Media or download) and the presentation file (.json, to reopen elsewhere with “⤒ Import”). A simple slideshow can become a presentation: “🎤 As a presentation” in the slideshow.

column2: How do I arrange or hide the presentation buttons and choose its starting settings?
column3: In the presentation, “⚙️ Customise”: each group of buttons at the top (insert, arrange, playback, file), the bar above the slides, the bottom bar, the inspector tabs and the sections of each tab (Position and size, Text, Image, Animations…) can be shown, hidden and arranged; a layout is kept under a name with “💾 Saved settings”. It is also in Settings → Montage, retouching, layout and sound (“🎤 Presentation” editor), with the theme, the format, the starting transition and layout, snapping, the colour of the laser pointer, full screen on opening and your own keyboard shortcuts.

column2: How do I restore an old damaged photo?
column3: Lists → Editing tools → Photo retouching → “🧭 Restore an old photo”, or in Retouch: the “🧭 Restore” tab (Image menu). Eight steps, each optional: straighten and crop; remove yellowing and revive the colours; find and remove dust and small spots automatically; fill scratches, creases and tears (healing brush, stamp); reduce grain; make a face sharper (surrounded with the ellipse); colourise (automatically, or with a brush and a palette of period tints); compare before / after and save as a new version (the original stays).

column2: How do I transcribe a record (baptism, marriage, death, notarial deed)?
column3: Lists → Editing tools → “📜 Record transcription”, or in an image viewer: “📜 Workshop”. The image of the record is on the left (zoom, contrast, negative, rotation), the text on the right (with old characters: ſ, œ, [illegible]…). Choose a passage then draw its area (▭ Area): a click on one highlights the other. “Read (printed)” reads a typed text and places the areas line by line; “✨ Read the record” reads handwriting (see the question “Read the record”). “🧭 Spot” finds the names and their role (godfather, witness, son of…), dates even written out in words (“l’an mil sept cent quatre-vingt-dix”) or in the Republican calendar (converted), places and occupations, and suggests the records that resemble them. “📋 Template” gives the outline of a record to complete.

column2: How do I change the size of an area in a record transcription?
column3: Click the area: it shows 8 handles (the corners and the middle of the sides). Pull a handle to change its size, drag the inside to move it; it does not leave the image and keeps a minimum size. With the keyboard: the arrows move it, Shift + arrows change its size, Alt to go point by point, Delete removes it (“↶ Undo” puts it back). ⌘Z undoes the last area change, ⇧⌘Z redoes it. The area stays linked to its passage in the text. It also works with the image rotated (⟳), straightened or mirrored, and with a finger (pinch to zoom).

column2: What is the ⤢ button for in record transcription?
column3: It changes how the image fits at each click: “Whole image” (you see the whole record), “Width” (the image takes the full width: best for reading a record from top to bottom), then “100 %” (actual size). The mode is written on the button; after zooming by hand (＋, －, the wheel or two fingers, always centred on the mouse or fingers), the button shows the percentage and a click returns to “Whole image”.

column2: How do I read a pale, yellowed or stained record better?
column3: In record transcription, the “🎚️ See better” settings: Sharpness (and its radius), Local contrast (brings out the writing everywhere, even in dark corners), Colour channel (All, Red, Green or Blue: brown ink often stands out better on blue), Remove the background (yellowing and stains disappear, the ink remains), Black and white threshold, Levels (black point, white point, gamma), Straighten to a tenth of a degree, Mirror (to read a text seen through the paper), Negative, Grey, and the 🔍 Magnifier that follows the mouse (the wheel changes the magnification; L key). “💾 Remember for this record” keeps these settings with the record; “↺ Original image” resets everything (with “↶ Undo”). Everything is calculated on your computer, without freezing the screen, even on a very large image. In “More ▾”, “Read and export the improved image” reads (printed or handwritten) and exports the image with these settings.

column2: How do I arrange the record transcription bar?
column3: With “⚙️” at the end of the bar, or in Settings → Montage, retouching, layout and sound → “📜 Record transcription: toolbar”. Two layouts: A (everything in the bar, which wraps onto a new line if needed) or B (a short bar and the “🎚️ See better ▾” panel, arranged into Bring out the ink, Black and white, Position, with a badge that counts the active settings). Tick what is shown, arrange with ↑ ↓ or by dragging ⠿, and in B choose what goes in the bar or in the panel. “↺ Reset to default” puts everything back as at the start; “💾 Saved settings” keeps a bar under a name. On a small screen, the settings go into “See better” by themselves.

column2: I can’t read an old record (Latin, abbreviations, long s): where can I find help?
column3: In record transcription, “📜 Reading help” (or Tools menu): first choose a word in the text, it is looked up automatically. Also: quick search (⌘K, type “filius”, “vve”, “dudit”…), ⋯ of the record, Settings → Glossary. Three tabs: 🔍 Dictionary (Latin of the registers, formulas for baptism, marriage and burial, abbreviations — including those of the censuses: cult., jlier, Vve, id., d° —, old words), filtered by kind and by record; ✍️ The letters (long s, round r, e and c, u and n, ligatures, barred p… drawn, with the letter not to be confused with); 🎓 Exercises: read a text written as in the register, type your reading, “✓ Correct” colours each word (right, to review with the explanation, forgotten, extra).

column2: How do I read a record in German, Italian, Spanish, Polish, Dutch, Latin or Greek?
column3: “📜 Help reading old records” (record transcription, quick search ⌘K, Settings → Glossary): at the top, the “Language” badges (with the number of words) keep a single language in the three tabs. 🔍 Dictionary: the words of baptism, marriage and death, the months (with the old names and 7bris, Xbre, Jänner, Hornung…), numbers and ages in words, occupations, kinship and whole formulas translated (“Im Jahre…”, “L’anno…”, “En la villa de…”, “Działo się…”, “Anno Domini…”). Type without accents: “malzonkowie” finds małżonkowie, “grossvater” Großvater; in Greek, write in Greek letters without accents or in Latin letters (“huios” finds υἱός). ✍️ The letters: German script (Kurrent, Sütterlin), the Greek alphabet and its handwritten forms, with a converter for Greek numbers (͵αωνβʹ = 1852). 🎓 Exercises: a model text per language, corrected word by word. In the transcription, choose the “Language of the text”: the help opens in that language, and “🧭 Spot” or “✨ Read the record” show the known words with their translation. The lists come from the FamilySearch “Word Lists” and from GenWiki.

column2: And for a record in Swedish, Danish, Norwegian, Czech, Slovak, Hungarian, Romanian, Croatian, Slovene, Lithuanian, or in Occitan, Breton, Basque?
column3: The same “📜 Help reading old records”: choose the language badge. For each: the words of baptism, marriage and death, the months (with the old names: Torsmånad, Boldogasszony hava, Gerar, svečan…), numbers and ages, occupations, kinship and translated formulas, plus a model exercise (example people) corrected word by word. Type without accents or signs: “szuletett” finds született, “brezna” března, “soen” Søn, “rodjen” rođen. Good to know: in Swedish, Danish and Norwegian, the surname changes with each generation (-son, -sen, -datter) and “aa” = å; in Hungarian, the surname comes before the first name (“Kovács Jánosné” = Mrs János Kovács); Danish counts in twenties (halvtreds = 50, a small converter is in the Dictionary); Romanian before 1860 is written in Cyrillic (alphabet in ✍️ The letters). Occitan, Breton and Basque are rare in registers: you will find them mostly in nicknames, place and house names, graves and a few notes by the priest.
